clue.text: An arc, as if tan — um? This is very cryptic!

definitions.text: An arc, as if tan — um? This is very cryptic!

parts.words: An arc, as if tan — um? This is very cryptic!
parts.note: respaced, the opening letters read AN ARC(A SIFT)ANUM: to sift is to sieve, so 'a sift' is a puzzle-word, and an arcanum, a deep secret, wraps round it

explanation.surface: Someone muses over an arc that looks tanned and admits the line makes no sense.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening words are not a phrase at all: run together and respaced they give A SIFT tucked inside AN ARCANUM, a riddle sitting within an enigma, which is what the answer phrase describes.
explanation.definitionFit: Churchill's famous description of Russia names something baffling layer upon layer, so it fits a thing that is very cryptic.

clue.text: Disgust dealing with lentil, say?

parts.note: RE means concerning or about, as in a letter heading
a lentil is an example of a pulse, an edible seed

explanation.surface: Someone is put off by a dish of lentils.
explanation.definitionFit: To disgust someone is to repel them, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Currency turning up around capital in Iraq?

definitions.text: Currency turning up around capital in Iraq?

indicators.note: around tells us one piece wraps the other
in a down answer, turning up means the word is read from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: the rand is South Africa's currency

indicators.note: the capital of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A query about money surfacing in the Iraqi capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning up' makes DNAR from RAND; 'around' puts it round I. The whole clue also defines the answer, Iraq's currency.
explanation.definitionFit: The dinar is the unit of money used in Iraq, so the whole clue describes it.

clue.text: Brief party outside the Church houses

indicators.note: houses means holds inside, so one piece contains the other

parts.note: laic means lay, belonging to the laity rather than the clergy
CON is short for the Conservative party

explanation.surface: A short note about a party that meets in buildings outside the church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outside the Church' is not a position: LAIC means lay, not of the clergy, and 'houses' holds the party inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Laconic speech uses very few words, so it is brief or terse.

clue.text: See 1
Breakfast item, more premature

definitions.meaning: a slice of bacon fried for the morning meal
the comparative of rash, acting too hastily

explanation.surface: A breakfast dish served too early.
explanation.definitionFit: A slice of bacon carries this name, and rash plus -er means hastier, acting before it is wise.

clue.text: Relevant page on internet refreshed

indicators.note: refreshing a web page reloads it; here the letters of internet are reloaded in a new order

explanation.surface: A relevant web page appears when the browser is refreshed.
explanation.definitionFit: Something pertinent bears directly on the matter in hand, a plain synonym of relevant.

clue.text: Since given time to plug rise of celebrity, film pioneer

indicators.note: plugging fills a gap, so these letters go inside the other piece
in a down answer, rise means the word is read upwards, backwards

parts.note: a celebrity is a big name

indicators.note: given means accompanied by, so the next piece is added

parts.note: as can mean since, as in 'as it was raining'

explanation.surface: A film pioneer became famous once time was spent promoting him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rise of' gives EMAN from NAME; 'to plug' puts AST inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: George Eastman founded Kodak and introduced roll film, making him an early pioneer of photography and cinema.

clue.text: Lesser eminence not entirely describing perfect maverick in poet

indicators.note: describing can mean drawing round, as a compass describes a circle, so it encloses the next pieces
not entirely means the last letter is cut off

parts.note: an eminence is a hill, so a lesser one is a small mound
A1 means first-rate, its digit read as the letter I
a maverick is a rebel who goes their own way

explanation.surface: A short hill is described within a poem about a perfect maverick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not entirely' cuts the K from HILLOCK; 'describing' wraps HILLOC round AIREBEL.
explanation.definitionFit: Hilaire Belloc was an Anglo-French writer best known for his Cautionary Tales in verse.

clue.text: See 1
Boy reportedly on bridge — checked

indicators.note: reportedly means as heard, so we use a word sounding like the name

parts.note: Chris is a boy's name
to bridge a gap is to cross it

explanation.surface: A boy on a bridge has been checked by someone.
explanation.definitionFit: A criss-cross pattern of crossing lines makes a check, like tartan.

clue.text: Buzz of social drinking?

indicators.note: of signals the answer is taken from within the following words

explanation.surface: The hum of chatter at a sociable drinks party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Buzz' looks like the noise of a party; it is the astronaut's first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Buzz is the first name of the astronaut who followed Armstrong onto the Moon in 1969.

clue.text: See 1
Over-the-top material fellow observed by playing charades

indicators.note: observed by means followed by, so the next piece comes after
playing a game of charades is acting it out; here the letters are played with and rearranged

explanation.surface: An outrageous fabric chap is watched by people playing charades.
explanation.walkthrough: 'playing' rearranges the letters of charades. 'Over-the-top' looks like 'excessive' but means worn on top of the head.
explanation.definitionFit: A headscarf is a piece of fabric worn over the top of the head.

clue.text: Fantastic wall with inscription of mark in concrete

indicators.note: an inscription is written into something, so the next piece goes inside

parts.note: a dike is an earth wall or bank

indicators.note: in puts this letter inside the next piece

parts.note: concrete means real, actual rather than abstract
M is short for mark, the old German currency

explanation.surface: A wonderful wall carved with a mark set in concrete.
explanation.walkthrough: M, the mark, is the old Deutschmark; 'concrete' here means real rather than the building material.
explanation.definitionFit: Something dreamlike is unreal and fanciful, as fantastic can mean.

clue.text: Copper like a writer?

definitions.meaning: a coin made of copper, the British cent-sized piece
read playfully as pen plus -y, having the quality of a pen

explanation.surface: A police officer resembling an author.
explanation.definitionFit: The British penny was once struck in copper, and adding -y to pen jokingly makes an adjective.

clue.text: One eaten by cannibal, due to ordering human takeaway?

indicators.note: ordering puts the letters into a new order

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I, and being eaten puts it inside the word cannibal; its exact place does not matter, as the letters are then rearranged

explanation.surface: A cannibal ordering a takeaway of human flesh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eaten by' tucks I into CANNIBAL; 'ordering' rearranges those letters with DUE TO. 'takeaway' suggests food, but it is a person taken away.
explanation.definitionFit: Aliens supposedly carry people off in a UFO, a whimsical kind of taking away of a human.

clue.text: Femme fatale lovelier, not very hideous

indicators.note: hideous suggests something misshapen, so the letters are put out of shape
not means the following letter is left out

explanation.surface: A seductive woman is lovelier, though not exactly ugly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' drops V from LOVELIER; 'hideous' rearranges LOELIER.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lorelei is the Rhine siren whose song lured boatmen to their deaths, a classic dangerous seductress.

clue.text: See 17
Just say before unloading lorry

indicators.note: before puts this piece ahead of the next

parts.note: to utter is to say

indicators.note: unloading empties the lorry, leaving only its outside letters

explanation.surface: Simply speak before emptying the truck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Just' looks like 'only' or 'fair', but here it is the intensifier.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are intensifying adverbs meaning completely, as in 'just wonderful'.

clue.text: Old writing, sound from pen?

parts.note: inking means writing in ink

explanation.surface: Old-fashioned writing, and the scratch of a nib.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pen' looks like the writing tool; it is a pigpen.
explanation.definitionFit: Pigs make this grunting noise, and pigs are kept in pens.

clue.text: Cap in deference then certainly lifted — like this?

definitions.text: Cap in deference then certainly lifted — like this?

indicators.note: the cap of a word is its first letter
in a down answer, lifted means the word is raised, read bottom to top

parts.note: deffo is British slang for definitely

explanation.surface: A hat raised respectfully, and certainly so.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lifted' turns DEFFO into OFFED. The whole clue describes a hat raised in respect.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking off a cap out of respect is exactly what a hat-raising gesture of deference is.

clue.text: Comic admits funny intro beaten

indicators.note: admits means lets in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: droll means amusing in a dry way
rum is British slang for odd or peculiar

explanation.surface: A comedian confesses that his amusing opening flopped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beaten' looks like 'defeated'; it means played on a drum.
explanation.definitionFit: A rapid roll on a drum is beaten out to introduce an act or announcement.

clue.text: Becoming rotten, though not in the middle — an old cracker?

indicators.note: the central letter of the word is taken out

parts.note: milk that is turning is going sour

explanation.surface: Something going off, though not fully, like a stale biscuit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cracker' suggests a biscuit; it is a codebreaker.
explanation.definitionFit: Alan Turing broke German Enigma codes at Bletchley Park in the Second World War.

clue.text: More than one spoke Russian and Arabic originally: 502?

indicators.note: originally points to the first letters of the words

parts.note: in Roman numerals D is 500 and II is 2

explanation.surface: Several speakers talked in Russian and Arabic, from room 502.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spoke' looks like the past of speak; it is a wheel's spoke.
explanation.definitionFit: Spokes of a wheel run from hub to rim, and these lines from a centre are the plural of radius.

clue.text: Powdered substance in blossom on tree, we hear?

indicators.note: we hear means the sound of the words is what matters

parts.note: a flower placed after a plane, the tree

explanation.surface: Pollen-like dust found in blooms on a tree.
explanation.definitionFit: Flour is finely ground grain, a powder, and plain flour has no raising agent.

clue.text: Murder: one covered up by Corleone, say?

indicators.note: covered up means hidden inside, so the letter goes within

parts.note: Vito Corleone of The Godfather is a Mafia don
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A killing hushed up by the Godfather's family.
explanation.definitionFit: To do someone in is an idiom for killing them.

clue.text: Untruth about alcoholic drink — it's non-alcoholic

indicators.note: about means going round, so one piece wraps the other

parts.note: a lie is an untruth
mead is a drink made from fermented honey

explanation.surface: A lie about a strong drink, which is really a soft one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'alcoholic drink' sits inside a clue whose definition is the opposite, non-alcoholic.
explanation.definitionFit: Limeade is a soft drink of lime juice and sugar, with no alcohol.

clue.text: My house accommodates an unknown knave

indicators.note: accommodates means takes in, so these letters go inside

parts.note: house is another name for bingo, and the call a winner makes
Y is a standard unknown in algebra
J is the jack, or knave, in cards

explanation.surface: My home puts up a mysterious rogue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My' looks like a possessive; it is an exclamation of surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are mild exclamations of surprise, as in 'My, what a view!'
